content: Golfer's elbow, also known as medial epicondylitis, is an inflammatory condition affecting the elbow. It shares some similarities with tennis elbow but involves different structures. The condition specifically affects the flexor muscles of the forearm, which are responsible for bending the fingers and thumb, clenching the fist, and supinating the hand (rotating the palm upward), excluding the biceps brachialis. These muscles converge into a common tendon that inserts into the medial epicondyle of the humerus at the elbow joint. When this tendon is subjected to minor injuries or, in some cases, without any apparent cause, the insertion site becomes inflamed. The term Golfer's elbow originates from the stress placed on this tendon during a golf swing. However, many individuals who develop this condition have never played golf. It is also occasionally referred to as Pitcher's elbow because the same tendon is stressed during activities like throwing a baseball, though this term is less commonly used. The primary symptom of Golfer's elbow is pain localized to the medial (inner) side of the elbow joint. This pain is significantly exacerbated when the flexor muscles of the forearm are under tension, although it may also occur at rest. Upon physical examination, the medial epicondyle of the humerus is extremely tender to touch. Additionally, there may be some weakness in the flexor muscles, which is not due to muscle damage but rather a reflex inhibition of their function caused by pain. Treatment for Golfer's elbow can include simple pain-relieving medications, as well as oral anti-inflammatory drugs. However, the most effective treatment involves the injection of a long-acting glucocorticoid (steroid) directly into and around the inflamed and tender area. While this injection may initially worsen symptoms for 24 to 48 hours, it typically leads to a resolution of the condition within five to seven days. It is crucial to avoid damaging the ulnar nerve during the injection process, as this nerve runs in the groove between the medial humeral epicondyle and the olecranon process of the ulna. For further reading, the condition known as tennis elbow, which affects the lateral side of the elbow, is related to Golfer's elbow.
